11. Theory of Sparse Regularization

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

The theory of sparse recovery asks when a reconstruction is unique, how much noise changes its coefficients, and whether it identifies the correct nonzero locations. A small reconstruction error alone does not guarantee that these locations are recovered. We use convex geometry and dual certificates to establish recovery conditions for the Lasso and its constrained counterpart, then examine their implications for spike deconvolution on increasingly fine grids.

11.1 Existence and Uniqueness¶

11.1.4 Uniqueness¶

The next proposition shows that at least one minimizer uses linearly independent columns of AAA. It does not assert that every minimizer has this property.

Proposition 11.4

For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, there is a solution x⋆x^\starx⋆ to (Pλ(y)\mathcal {P}_\lambda (y)Pλ​(y)) whose support III satisfies ker⁡(AI)={0}\ker(A_I)=\{0\}ker(AI​)={0}. The same holds for (P0(y)\mathcal {P}_0(y)P0​(y)) when it is feasible.

Proof

Let xxx be a minimizer and I=supp(x)I=\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}(x)I=supp(x). If AIA_IAI​ is not injective, choose a nonzero hI∈ker⁡(AI)h_I\in\ker(A_I)hI​∈ker(AI​) and extend it by zero outside III. Along the interval containing t=0t=0t=0 on which x+thx+thx+th retains the sign of xxx, the fidelity is constant and the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 norm is affine. Optimality at the interior point t=0t=0t=0 forces its slope to vanish. Move to a finite endpoint of this interval, where at least one coefficient becomes zero. Continuity shows that the endpoint is still a minimizer and has smaller support. Repeating the argument terminates after finitely many steps at a minimizer with injective AIA_IAI​.

If the columns of AIA_IAI​ on a minimizer’s support are linearly dependent, the proof constructs another minimizer. Thus that solution of (Pλ(y)\mathcal {P}_\lambda (y)Pλ​(y)) is nonunique.

Although the coefficient vector xλx_\lambdaxλ​ may not be unique, its fitted data AxλAx_\lambdaAxλ​, also called the predictor, are unique.

Multiplying (11.4) by the restricted measurement matrix gives

Axλ=ProjIm(AI)y−λAI(AI∗AI)−1sign(xλ,I).(11.5)A x_{\lambda} = \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(A_I)} y - \lambda A_I (A_I^*A_I)^{-1} \mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(x_{\lambda,I}). \tag{11.5}Axλ​=ProjIm(AI​)​y−λAI​(AI∗​AI​)−1sign(xλ,I​).(11.5)

11.1.5 Duality¶

The first-order conditions can also be derived from the convex duality theory in Section 18.3. This interpretation explains why certificates characterize optimal recovery.

Theorem 11.8

For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, strong duality holds between (Pλ(y)\mathcal {P}_\lambda (y)Pλ​(y)) and the following dual problem. For λ=0\lambda=0λ=0, the same statement holds with (P0(y)\mathcal {P}_0(y)P0​(y)) as the primal problem, provided y∈Im(A)y\in\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(A)y∈Im(A):

This theorem guarantees uniqueness of the noiseless solution x0x_0x0​, but does not imply uniqueness of xλx_\lambdaxλ​.

The source condition (11.13), combined with the injectivity condition ker⁡(AJ)={0}\ker(A_{J})=\{0\}ker(AJ​)={0}, gives the ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2 stability estimate (11.14).

The estimate (11.14) controls the error linearly relative to the fixed noiseless signal x0x_0x0​. It does not by itself establish pairwise Lipschitz continuity between arbitrary noisy solutions.

Compare this linear rate with the sublinear rates for quadratic regularization in Theorem 9.4.

The source conditions for linear regularization (9.12) and nonlinear regularization (11.13) express different structural assumptions.

In the quadratic case with β=1\beta=1β=1, the source condition is x0∈Im(A∗)=ker⁡(A)⊥x_0\in\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(A^*)=\ker(A)^\botx0​∈Im(A∗)=ker(A)⊥ in finite dimension. The signal itself must have no component in ker⁡(A)\ker(A)ker(A) because squared-norm regularization cannot recover such a component.

The nonlinear condition instead requires a subgradient η\etaη to belong to Im(A∗)\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(A^*)Im(A∗). It can therefore permit recovery of signal components in ker⁡(A)\ker(A)ker(A) when the prior supplies sufficient structure.

11.2.3 Sparsistency for Low Noise¶

Theorem 11.11 gives an abstract guarantee whose certificate assumptions may be difficult to verify.

We now construct a candidate certificate explicitly. When it satisfies a strict off-support bound, it guarantees both a linear rate and support stability.

For any solution xλx_\lambdaxλ​ of (Pλ(y))(\mathcal{P}_\lambda(y))(Pλ​(y)), define the dual certificate as in (11.2). Uniqueness of the fitted data makes it independent of the chosen solution:

The next proposition shows that pλp_\lambdapλ​ converges to the dual solution of minimum norm for the constrained problem.

Theorem 11.15 requires small correlated noise ∣ ⁣∣A∗w∣ ⁣∣∞|\!| A^*w |\!|_\infty∣∣A∗w∣∣∞​ and a small λ\lambdaλ, with their ratio controlled, so that regularization does not eliminate the nonzero coefficients of x0x_0x0​. Theorem 11.11, by contrast, applies at any noise level ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣|\!| w |\!|∣∣w∣∣, but gives neither support control nor uniqueness of xλx_\lambdaxλ​, and its constants can be less favorable.

The proof provides explicit constants in terms of three parameters K,L,SK,L,SK,L,S:

  • KKK accounts for the conditioning of the operator on the support III;

  • LLL is the largest sum of absolute correlations between an off-support atom and all atoms on the support;

  • SSS measures the margin by which ηF\eta_FηF​ avoids saturation outside the support.

The bounds on ∣ ⁣∣A∗w∣ ⁣∣∞/λ|\!| A^*w |\!|_\infty/\lambda∣∣A∗w∣∣∞​/λ and on λ\lambdaλ are given by (11.22). For fixed γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 and sufficiently small δ>0\delta>0δ>0, choosing λ=(1+γ)Rδ/S\lambda=(1+\gamma)R\delta/Sλ=(1+γ)Rδ/S gives

∣ ⁣∣x0−xλ∣ ⁣∣∞⩽K(1+(1+γ)RS)δ.|\!| x_0-x_\lambda |\!|_\infty\leqslant K\left(1+(1+\gamma)\frac{R}{S}\right)\delta.∣∣x0​−xλ​∣∣∞​⩽K(1+(1+γ)SR​)δ.

The strict factor 1+γ1+\gamma1+γ ensures the required strict inequality. Such a choice is primarily theoretical because its constants involve the unknown support.

For a class of signals x0x_0x0​, analyzing ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 support recovery therefore starts with testing the Fuchs precertificate ηF\eta_FηF​: feasibility requires ∣ ⁣∣ηF∣ ⁣∣∞⩽1|\!| \eta_F |\!|_\infty \leqslant 1∣∣ηF​∣∣∞​⩽1, and support stability requires a strict bound outside the support.

Figure 11.9 illustrates the behavior for random AAA: the precertificate ηF\eta_FηF​ becomes nondegenerate when PPP is sufficiently large. Section 12.2 analyzes this phenomenon.

11.2.4 Sparsistency for Arbitrary Noise¶

The small-noise theorem fixes the sign of the solution in advance. To obtain support containment for arbitrary noise levels, one can instead control all sign patterns on a prescribed support III. This gives the exact recovery coefficient of Tropp [32]:

ERC⁡(I)=1−max⁡j∉I∣ ⁣∣AI+aj∣ ⁣∣1.\operatorname{ERC}(I)=1-\max_{j\notin I}|\!| A_I^+a_j |\!|_1.ERC(I)=1−j∈/Imax​∣∣AI+​aj​∣∣1​.

The maximum over an empty complement is taken to be zero. Assume AIA_IAI​ is injective and ERC⁡(I)>0\operatorname{ERC}(I)>0ERC(I)>0. Let PI=AIAI+P_I=A_IA_I^+PI​=AI​AI+​ and choose λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 so that

∣ ⁣∣AIc∗(Id−PI)y∣ ⁣∣∞<λERC⁡(I).|\!| A_{I^c}^*(\mathrm{Id}-P_I)y |\!|_\infty <\lambda\operatorname{ERC}(I).∣∣AIc∗​(Id−PI​)y∣∣∞​<λERC(I).

Then the Lasso has a unique solution supported within III; some coefficients may vanish, so equality of supports is not asserted.

Indeed, minimize the Lasso objective over vectors supported on III. The resulting vector x^I\hat x_Ix^I​ is unique, since AIA_IAI​ is injective. Its optimality condition gives qI∈∂∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣1(x^I)q_I\in\partial|\!| \cdot |\!|_1(\hat x_I)qI​∈∂∣∣⋅∣∣1​(x^I​) and

y−AIx^I=(Id−PI)y+λAI(AI∗AI)−1qI.y-A_I\hat x_I=(\mathrm{Id}-P_I)y+\lambda A_I(A_I^*A_I)^{-1}q_I.y−AI​x^I​=(Id−PI​)y+λAI​(AI∗​AI​)−1qI​.

For j∉Ij\notin Ij∈/I, the corresponding dual coefficient is bounded by

∣⟨aj,(Id−PI)y⟩∣λ+∣ ⁣∣AI+aj∣ ⁣∣1<1.\frac{|\langle a_j,(\mathrm{Id}-P_I)y\rangle|}{\lambda} +|\!| A_I^+a_j |\!|_1<1.λ∣⟨aj​,(Id−PI​)y⟩∣​+∣∣AI+​aj​∣∣1​<1.

Thus the restricted minimizer satisfies the full optimality conditions with strict inequality outside III, and injectivity proves uniqueness. If y=Ax0+wy=Ax_0+wy=Ax0​+w and supp(x0)⊂I\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}(x_0)\subset Isupp(x0​)⊂I, the orthogonal residual above is (Id−PI)w(\mathrm{Id}-P_I)w(Id−PI​)w. The condition therefore states explicitly how large λ\lambdaλ must be relative to the noise.

For random AAA, Chapter 12 gives probabilistic conditions under which ηF\eta_FηF​ is a valid certificate.

Super-resolution exposes a limitation of the Fuchs construction. The columns (ai)i(a_i)_i(ai​)i​ of AAA are often samples of a smooth kernel, so nearby columns are highly correlated.

We consider ai=φ(zi)a_i=\varphi(z_i)ai​=φ(zi​), where (zi)i⊂X(z_i)_i \subset \mathbb{X}(zi​)i​⊂X is a sampling grid in a domain X\mathbb{X}X and φ:X→H\varphi: \mathbb{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{H}φ:X→H is a smooth map. One has

Ax=∑ixiφ(zi).A x = \sum_i x_i \varphi(z_i).Ax=i∑​xi​φ(zi​).

Evaluating η~V=A∗pV\tilde\eta_V=\mathcal{A}^*p_Vη~​V​=A∗pV​ on the reconstruction grid gives the discrete precertificate ηV\eta_VηV​.

Figure 11.11 shows better behavior of ηV\eta_VηV​ than of ηF\eta_FηF​. If ∣ ⁣∣ηV∣ ⁣∣∞⩽1|\!| \eta_V |\!|_\infty\leqslant 1∣∣ηV​∣∣∞​⩽1 and AAA is injective on its saturation set, Theorem 11.11 gives a linear rate in the grid-based ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2 norm. As the grid is refined, however, this coefficient ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2 norm does not provide an intrinsic distance between spike measures, which need not have L2L^2L2 densities.

When ηV\eta_VηV​ differs from ηF\eta_FηF​, one cannot directly apply Theorem 11.15: exact support stability on increasingly fine grids can fail in super-resolution problems.

Methods without a fixed grid provide a more suitable framework for such stability results. In a grid-free formulation, a valid vanishing-derivative precertificate coincides with the minimum-norm certificate under the corresponding interpolation and nondegeneracy assumptions. This leads to stability results for spike locations and amplitudes, rather than a fixed-grid coefficient norm.
